Consult Summary:
- Telemedicine consult for 6-week history of left-sided decreased hearing with intermittent unilateral tinnitus and mild off-balance sensation; plan for in-person otoscopic evaluation within 4–5 days and provision of tinnitus education.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Reduced hearing in the left ear.
- Duration/onset: ~6 weeks; prior brief similar episode ~1 year ago lasting a couple of days.
- Course: Intermittent over the 6 weeks.
- Laterality: Left ear only; right ear “seems fine.”
- Associated symptoms:
  - Intermittent ringing (tinnitus) in the left ear.
  - Occasional mild dizziness/off-balance; not room-spinning; described as “nothing major.” Earlier noted feeling “a bit sick” at times.
  - Denies ear pain.
  - Denies fever.
  - Denies chest pain.
  - Palpitations: not documented.
  - Ear discharge: clinician confirmed “No.”
  - Ear itch: not documented.
- Triggers/relievers:
  - Patient stated “some things trigger it,” giving examples of watching TV/listening to music; also stated that these “solve the ringing.” Conflict noted regarding the effect of sound exposure on tinnitus.
- Prior care: None documented.
- Education provided: Tinnitus discussed; clinician will provide a patient information leaflet link to review before in-person visit.

Past Medical History:
- Not documented.

Social History:
- Denies using cotton swabs to clean ears.
- Other social factors (tobacco, alcohol, substances, occupation): not documented.

Family History:
- Not documented.

Physical Examination:
- 

Investigations:
- None completed during this video visit.
- Planned: In-person otoscopic examination within 4–5 days to assess for cerumen impaction or other ear pathology.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Left-sided decreased hearing with unilateral tinnitus (intermittent) and mild non-vertiginous dizziness
  - Assessment: 6-week history; no ear pain or discharge; intermittent tinnitus; mild off-balance without true vertigo; right ear subjectively normal. Differential includes conductive cause (e.g., cerumen impaction) versus middle/inner ear pathology. No acute red flags reported in transcript.
  - Plan:
    - Schedule face-to-face appointment within 4–5 days for otoscopy to rule out cerumen impaction or other physical blockage.
    - If cerumen impaction present, address accordingly; if ear exam is normal, consider further evaluation for middle/inner ear or balance system etiologies as clinically indicated.
    - Provide tinnitus patient information leaflet link for review prior to visit.
    - Advise to contact the clinic if any problems arise before the appointment or if symptoms worsen.
- Issue 2: Administrative coordination
  - Plan:
    - Clinician to message admin team to arrange booking within 4–5 days; patient to call support team (number placed in appointment notes) to confirm scheduling.

General plan items:
- Not an emergency per clinician; proceed with planned in-person evaluation.
- Follow-up: With another GP in the clinic within 4–5 days; earlier video review if issues arise.

Quality checks (always include at bottom of note, or fill document_quality):
- Missing expected elements: Allergies not documented; current medications not documented; past medical/surgical history not documented; comprehensive social history (tobacco/alcohol/substances) not documented; vitals not obtained; physical exam not performed; family history not documented.
- Internal conflicts:
  - Name discrepancy: Patient identified as “Jack Smith,” but clinician addressed patient as “John.” Conflict noted.
  - Symptom trigger inconsistency: Patient stated TV/music “trigger” tinnitus and also that they “solve the ringing.” Conflict noted.
  - Nausea inconsistency: Early comment of feeling “a bit sick” versus later description of dizziness “not the kind with nausea.” Conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear, with minor incomplete/unclear phrases; some yes/no responses implied rather than explicitly stated.
